description: Cluster 1, delineating a thematic focus on sustainability, encapsulates 980 scholarly articles with a cumulative citation count of 62,323. This cluster primarily supports SDG 12 (responsible consumption and production) and represents a substantive contribution to the understanding of sustainability-related subjects, furnishing noteworthy insights for prospective research undertakings in this sphere. As noted earlier in Sect. 3.5., among the highly cited works, the study by York et  al. (2003) refines the STIRPAT model through the incorporation of ecological elasticity, population, modernization, affluence, and environmental factors to attain sustainability. Further, Wackernagel et  al. (1999) present a framework for natural capital accounting, employing the ecological footprint concept to compare human consumption with natural capital production and assess sustainability at both national and global context. In a parallel vein, Wu (2014) reviews the evolution of urban ecology highlighting the pivotal role of cities in global sustainability and stresses the need for a comprehensive framework to steer urban development towards sustainable trajectories. Another significant contribution to this cluster is the study by Tononi et al. (2017), which reveals the challenges faced by cities for the attainment of a sustainable future, suggesting local sustainable strategies, enhanced citizen participation, and the critical role of community engagement in urban sustainability. Rérat (2021) examines the mobility practices at the University of Lausanne and discovers that the efficiency of university transport and parking policies help transform the university into a sustainable community (SDG 11).

The cluster focused on renewable energy supporting SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy), contains a sizable body of literature encompassing 411 publications and 29,104 citations. In an influential work, Ahmed et al. (2020) investigate the complicated interplay between natural resource abundance, human capital, urbanization, and ecological footprint and disclose that natural resources and urbanization amplify environmental degradation, while human capital helps mitigate these effects. Another significant contribution by Danish et al. (2020) features the fundamental role of renewable energy, urbanization, and natural resource rent on ecological footprint and environmental quality. Khan et al. (2021) also validate the significant impact of natural resources, energy consumption, and population growth on environmental sustainability. Besides the environmental benefits, renewable energy provides opportunities for greater energy independence and empowers countries with limited access to traditional energy resources to generate their own energy (Tutak & Brodny, 2022). Kazak et al. (2023) frame their research on the concepts of energy justice and ecological debt to probe the involvement of Polish communities in energy transition to achieve renewable energy balance and thereby sustainability. The study finds significant inconsistencies between communities in terms of renewable energy adoption, with only 29% of communities could achieve and exceed their energy needs, while 71% remain energy debtors owing to deficient financial and infrastructure support. Additionally, Sibt-e-Ali et al. (2024) suggest that increased investments in renewable energy and green technologies promote sustainable development in emerging countries. Dam et al. (2024) investigate E-7 countries and discover that technological innovation and renewable energy reduce the ecological footprint, supporting SDGs 7 and 13. Shabir et al. (2023) analyzing OECD countries, reveal that renewable energy and energy innovation mitigate ecological footprint and stress greater investment in green energy policies. Similarly, Aneja et al. (2023) highlight the critical role of clean energy and green technology in mitigating environmental degradation in their study on G-20 nations.

EKC, which supports SDG 8 (decent work and economic growth), appears as a prominent theme of third cluster with 256 publications and 24,739 citations. Among significant contributors in this cluster, Destek and Sarkodi (2019) validate the EKC hypothesis by discovering the association between economic growth, energy consumption, financial development, and ecological footprint in industrialized countries. The results confirm an inverted U-shaped relationship between ecological footprint and economic growth. In a similar vein, Al-Mulali et  al. (2015) investigate the relationship between ecological footprint and GDP in the case of high-income countries and deliver empirical support for the EKC hypothesis. Further, Ulucak and Bilgili (2018), verify the EKC hypothesis studying ecological footprint across countries from varied income groups. The cluster also shed light on sub-topics, such as the impact of trade openness on the environment (Al-Mulali & Ozturk, 2015; Charfeddine, 2017) and the complex relationship between environmental degradation and human capital (Danish et al., 2019; Zafar et al., 2019).

The fourth cluster centers around tourism with 37 scholarly articles that receive a total of 3341 citations. In a significant inquiry, Lee and Brahmasrene (2013) uncover complex interconnections among tourism, CO2 emissions, foreign direct investment (FDI), and economic growth. Ozturk et al. (2016) investigate the EKC hypothesis and further advance this cluster by reflecting the need to address environmental concerns alongside tourism development. Additionally, Gössling et al. (2002) present a framework for calculating the ecological footprint of leisure tourism, highlighting themes related to measurement challenges, energy in air travel, impacts on greenhouse inventories, and the potential of tourism to conserve biodiversity. Sustainable ecotourism emerges as the latest research theme in this cluster. In this direction, Palli et al. (2023) emphasize on the significant role of tour guides in creating environmental awareness among stakeholders (i.e., park managers, local communities, and tourists) and determine that training tour guides helps to achieve sustainable environmental objectives. Community-based tourism (CBT) emerge as another significant theme as highlighted by He et al. (2021), who disclose essential criteria to assess the utility of CBT, including training and education, stakeholder involvement, and community participation to achieve sustainability. Pasanchay and Schott (2021), in a similar context, identify the key role of CBT for achieving the SDGs, particularly related to poverty reduction (SDG 1) and the maintenance of sustainable communities and societies (SDG 11).

The concept of human well-being, related to SDG 3 (good health and well-being), emerges as a prominent concept in the fifth cluster comprising 35 scholarly articles and 3,250 citations. The seminal work by Kassouri and Altıntaş (2020) investigates the conflicting relationship between human development and ecological footprint as sustainability indicators and divulges the significant role of economic institutions to bring a balance between human well-being and ecological protection. Bravo (2014) updates the United Nation’s Human Development Index (HDI) and presents Human Sustainable Development Index (HSDI) to capture environmental sustainability. The study concludes that HSDI remains insufficient despite its advantages over HDI and advises to develop an index integrating social, economic, and environmental features to measure sustainable development. Another significant contribution to this cluster is the study by Zhang et al. (2018), which outlines the Index of Ecological Well-being Performance (IEWP) to quantify the impact of ecological consumption on human well-being and to discover ecologically efficient countries. These studies recognize the importance of integrating environmental impact into human development measures to effectively promote sustainable development. In addition, Kubiszewski et  al., (2013) study genuine progress indicator (GPI) as a human well-being measure in comparison with the gross domestic product (GDP) and conclude that despite GPI is not an ideal economic welfare measurement tool, it is acceptable as compared to the GDP. Contributing to recent developments in the human well-being theme, Patrick et al. (2021) emphasize the need for the Happy Planet Index (HPI) to measure the relationship between human health and the health of the environment at a local level and advocate the promotion of community engagement for the achievement of environmental sustainability and human well-being. This cluster also accentuates the professional contributions of social workers in collaboration with homeless people and marginalized groups for environmental justice and human well-being (Dominelli, 2013). Furthermore, Grose and Richardson (2016) highlight the crucial role of sustainable education to enhance skills and practice-based behavior among health care professionals to reduce ecological footprint of health services.

The sixth cluster with 26 articles and 2270 citations, revolves around the concept of convergence analysis and offers a deeper understanding of the convergent phenomenon, policy shocks, and vital sustainability features aligned with SDG 10 (reduced inequalities). In this cluster, following the club clustering methodological approach Ulucak and Apergis (2018) investigate the convergence of the per capita ecological footprint and verify the presence of convergence clubs in the member countries of European Union (EU). The study clarifies their differences in terms of environmental quality, and outlines awareness strategies suitable for them keeping into account their diverse structures. Likewise, Ulucak and Lin (2017) investigate the policy shocks to ecological footprint in the USA and suggest policies with renewable energy use to permanently contain ecological footprint in the long run. Similarly, Solarin and Bello (2018) examine the stationarity of ecological footprint for 128 countries and find that policies such as imposition of a carbon tax, subsidies for cleaner energy, and appropriate land use act will have long-term and permanent effects on the ecological footprint in many countries. Wood et al. (2021) argue that building sustainable future that ‘leave no one behind’ requires to understand global challenges, anticipate risks and opportunities, and engage diverse communities to exercise collective foresight and share perspectives to arrive at informed decision-making at all levels. The concept of environmental convergence enhances stakeholder and community engagement and offers a common platform to assess and advance the progress of collective sustainability efforts aligned with SDG 17 (partnerships for the goals).

Cluster seven consists of three key studies by Ke et al., (2020, 2021, 2022), collectively accumulating 560 citations. These studies highlight that while innovation efficiency can initially decrease the ecological footprint, its effects vary regionally and are influenced by factors such as economic development and industrialization. This suggests that targeted policy interventions are essential for improving sustainability outcomes across diverse geographical and economic contexts to achieve SDG 9 (industry, innovation, and infrastructure). Taken together with the findings from the cluster related to renewable energy, this cluster emphasizes the paramount necessity for the development of a sustainable innovation model, which considers regional specificities and ensures territorial cooperation to achieve sustainable development. D’Adamo et al. (2024) also suggest establishing such a model and argue that it can offer competitive advantage when combined with global resources and skills.
